spiced.situation: Matt is Co-Founder and COO at FlatPeak. He has been aware of ISO 27001 for some time — this is the second contact, with the first call in October 2025 and a follow-up in May 2026. ISO certification has been on his radar but has not progressed. He has personal prior experience with ISO 27001, describing having 'gone through it enough times' before, which means he is not coming in blind. The company appears to be in a growth phase, fielding increasing questions from customers about certification.
spiced.pain: Matt is experiencing what he described as 'creeping, increasing questions from customers' about ISO certification. There is no acute crisis, but the pressure is building from the customer base rather than from any internal deadline. He is also sceptical about the value of the process itself, having characterised ISO 27001 as '85% box ticking and 10% actual usefulness' — suggesting his pain includes a frustration with the bureaucratic weight of certification, not just the absence of it. He is time-poor and has deprioritised this repeatedly despite acknowledging it needs doing.
spiced.impact: The growing customer enquiries signal that the absence of ISO 27001 is becoming a friction point in commercial conversations — consistent with the SDR's pitch about it being 'a bit of a bottleneck to bring in more revenue.' While Matt did not explicitly confirm lost deals, the pattern of customers asking 'that sort of thing' suggests it is increasingly affecting trust or eligibility in enterprise or regulated client conversations. The strategic risk is that continued delay allows this to compound as FlatPeak moves upmarket.
spiced.critical_event: No hard deadline was mentioned. Matt explicitly said 'there's no deadlines.' However, he did say he would like to get certification done this year (2026), and the meeting has been booked for the last week of June 2026. The SDR flagged that the typical process takes three to six months, which Matt did not push back on — meaning if he wants certification by end of year, the window to start is narrowing. This is a soft urgency lever the AE can use, not a genuine critical event.
spiced.decision: Matt appears to be the primary decision-maker and likely holds sign-off given his Co-Founder and COO title. He referred to 'a couple of things we need to sort out first' without naming other stakeholders, suggesting he is driving this himself. There is no indication of a formal procurement process, committee, or budget cycle. He did mention he has 'a list of a couple of people I want to speak to properly' before deciding, which implies he is comparing providers. No budget figure or approval process was discussed.

objections.objection: Not the right time — repeatedly pushed back timing across two calls, first to Q2, then to end of year, then to last week of June.
objections.response: The SDR handled this reasonably well by not forcing urgency but did plant the three-to-six month timeline as a soft nudge. The meeting was eventually booked by suggesting a scoping conversation rather than a sales meeting, which lowered the barrier. However, the SDR did not probe what the 'couple of things to sort out first' actually were, which is a gap the AE needs to address.

objections.objection: Scepticism about the value of ISO 27001 — described it as '85% box ticking and 10% actual usefulness' and implied the process is largely template-driven.
objections.response: This objection was not addressed at all in either call. The SDR did not challenge or reframe this view. This is the most significant unhandled objection going into the meeting. Matt will likely come in with a transactional mindset, expecting a cheap, fast, templated job. The AE needs to either validate this efficiently and show how ISO Serious delivers exactly that, or carefully reframe where genuine value sits without being preachy about it.

objections.objection: Requested email material rather than committing to a conversation on the first call.
objections.response: The SDR handled this acceptably by keeping the door open and securing a callback permission, which eventually led to the May follow-up call and the booked meeting.

handovers.recommended_approach: Open by acknowledging the history — Matt knows who you are, you have spoken twice, and he knows this has been on the back burner. Do not treat this as a cold introduction. Start by validating his situation directly: something like, 'You mentioned customers are increasingly asking for this — I wanted to understand what that looks like for you in practice before we talk about anything on our side.' This gets him talking about commercial reality before you pitch anything. The most important thing to probe is what the 'couple of things to sort out first' actually are — these may be internal blockers, competing priorities, or even a co-founder who needs convincing. You need to know whether those blockers have been resolved or whether this meeting is still premature. His '85% box ticking' comment is the framing he will arrive with, so get ahead of it early. Do not be defensive. Instead, use it as an opening: ask him what his previous experience looked like and what he would want to be different this time. This positions ISO Serious as a pragmatic, efficient operator rather than a consultancy trying to inflate scope. Frame the conversation around speed to certification and minimal internal disruption — he wants this done, not drawn out. Use the three-to-six month window the SDR mentioned to create gentle urgency: if he wants this wrapped up in 2026, the conversation is timely. Do not oversell. Matt is experienced, sceptical, and comparing providers. Come in as a peer who is helping him make a practical decision, not a salesperson trying to close him.

spiced.situation: Matt Roderick is Co-Founder and COO at FlatPeak. ISO 27001 certification has been on the company's radar since at least January 2026, when Matt and the SDR first spoke. It has not progressed — he described it as still on a list of things to do but not having moved up it. There is no indication of a formal project, dedicated owner, or existing compliance framework in place. The company appears to be at an early, pre-commitment stage with no process formally underway.
spiced.pain: Matt is not experiencing an acute internal pain point that he himself has articulated in strong terms. However, the underlying driver is external pressure from customers: he specifically said there are 'creeping, increasing questions from customers' about ISO 27001. This suggests that prospects or existing clients are beginning to make certification a condition of doing business, or at minimum are scrutinising FlatPeak's security posture more regularly. The pain is reputational and commercial rather than operational — they are being asked to evidence something they cannot yet evidence.
spiced.impact: The impact is primarily commercial. If customer questions about ISO certification are increasing, FlatPeak risks losing deals or failing to progress enterprise conversations where ISO 27001 is a procurement requirement. There is no stated lost deal or specific revenue figure, but the direction of travel is clear: the longer certification is delayed, the more exposed they become to being disqualified by security-conscious buyers. There may also be a reputational dimension if they are seen as lacking maturity relative to competitors who are already certified.
spiced.critical_event: No hard deadline was mentioned. Matt explicitly said 'there's no deadlines.' The softer driver is the accumulation of customer questions, which creates a slow-burn urgency rather than a fixed trigger. He did say he would like to get it done this year, which implies a loose target of completing certification before end of 2026. Given that the SDR noted ISO 27001 typically takes three to six months, a conversation in late June would need to result in a relatively prompt start to achieve certification within 2026.
spiced.decision: Matt is Co-Founder and COO, which suggests he is likely one of the primary decision-makers. He referred to 'a couple of things we need to sort out first' before progressing ISO certification, implying there are internal dependencies or competing priorities, possibly involving his co-founder. No mention was made of a procurement process, budget sign-off requirements, or other stakeholders. However, given he is a co-founder, it is reasonable to assume any significant spend would involve at least one other founder-level conversation. This was not explored on the call.

objections.objection: It's still on the list but hasn't moved — there are other things to sort out first.
objections.response: The SDR acknowledged this and moved on without probing what those blocking items are or what would need to happen for ISO to move up the priority list. This is a significant gap. The AE does not know what the competing priorities are or what would unlock forward movement.

objections.objection: Preference to defer — asked the SDR to just send an email and he would call back when ready.
objections.response: The SDR handled this reasonably well by pivoting to suggest a short-term scoping conversation rather than simply agreeing to wait. Matt accepted the reframe and agreed to a meeting in the last week of June. However, the SDR framed the meeting as exploratory and low-stakes ('outline expectations, ask a few questions'), which may undersell the value of the conversation to Matt.

handovers.recommended_approach: Open by acknowledging that this is deliberately a no-pressure conversation — Matt agreed to it on that basis and will be sensitive to feeling sold to before he is ready. Frame the meeting as genuinely diagnostic: you are there to understand where FlatPeak is today and help Matt think through what the path to certification actually looks like in practical terms, so that when they do decide to move, they are not starting from zero. From there, probe hard on the customer questions angle — this is the real commercial nerve. Ask which types of customers are raising ISO questions, whether it has come up in any live deals or renewals, and whether any opportunity has been lost or stalled as a result. This will help Matt connect the delay to real revenue risk rather than treating it as an abstract compliance task. Also probe what the 'couple of things to sort out first' actually are — if those are blockers, the AE needs to understand them. If they are unrelated, Matt may not have fully considered that ISO work could run in parallel. Clarify who else would need to be involved in a decision to proceed — the co-founder relationship is unexplored and could be a hidden veto. On timeline, gently surface the three-to-six-month point the SDR mentioned: if Matt wants this done in 2026 and the meeting is end of June, the window is tight. Use that as a natural reason to think concretely about next steps rather than leaving it open-ended again. Avoid making this feel like a closing meeting — Matt's trust has been built on the basis that this is a scoping conversation, and that framing should be respected.
